column2: Lectures L13 (international trade) and L14 (platforms, auctions), linked to the past exams 2020–2025. Rebuild the decisions, relative prices and rules before calculating.

You may get trade, a platform, an auction or a snack exchange. These topics appear in the past exams and are covered in lectures L13 (international trade) and L14 (platforms and auctions). Each tool from the lectures is linked to the exam questions where it appeared.

L13 (Friberg 17.1–17.3): comparative advantage, specific factors, trade policy. L14 (Friberg 18.1–18.3): platforms and auctions. Edgeworth comes from dossier §14.6. Exam links: trade E2020, E2021, E2022, E2024, E2025; auctions E2023, E2025; platforms E2022, E2025.
According to lecture L14, which part of the course does the exam emphasise?
The second part, after L6
L14: 4 questions (+ one question that replaces the midterm), emphasis on the end of the course.
Only chapters 1 to 3
The lecture says the opposite: the emphasis is on the second half.
Only definitions, without figures
The lecture asks for clear and precise figures and discussion.
A tariff is just one of several tools for curbing imports

A government can tax imports, limit their quantity, subsidise its exporters or simply make the paperwork harder. Standards or patents can also hold back trade without being called a “tariff”. Each tool protects a specific group; the question is who pays.

Lecture L13: tariffs, quotas, export subsidies, “red tape”, plus domestic policies with a trade dimension (standards, intellectual property, support for national firms, competition). Frameworks: WTO, free trade areas, customs unions, EU.
A concentrated group (protected producers) gains a lot per head and organises; the loss is spread thinly over all consumers.
Supporting a sector's employees is usually better done through transfers than through a tariff, which adds the two deadweight losses.

L13 sorts the reasons into three groups: special interests (harmful to national welfare), reasons useful for one country but not the world (Airbus versus Boeing, infant industries), reasons potentially useful globally (national security, avoiding a race to the bottom in standards).
In the exam, if asked “why do tariffs exist?”, structure your answer: who gains, at the level of the country or the world, and is there a better tool?
Which of these arguments can improve world welfare, not only national welfare?
Avoiding a race to the bottom in environmental standards
L13 lists it among the reasons potentially favourable to the whole world.
Helping Airbus against Boeing
A possible gain for one country at the expense of foreign firms: not a global gain.
Protecting the profits of a well-organised sector
A special interest: usually harmful to national welfare.
The side that attracts the other pays less, sometimes nothing

A rental platform earns money on every renter and every owner. But one more renter makes the platform more valuable to all owners. Charging that renter a lot also means losing what they bring to the other side.
Lecture L14: v_b = f_b n_s − p_b, π_s = f_s n_b − p_s; profit n_s(p_s − c_s) + n_b(p_b − c_b). Optimal prices: p_b = (c_b − f_s n_s)·ε_b/(ε_b − 1) and p_s = (c_s − f_b n_b)·ε_s/(ε_s − 1).
The relevant “cost” of a buyer is c_b minus the value f_s n_s they create for sellers: if they create a lot, this effective cost turns negative and the price can too.
As for a monopoly, the factor ε/(ε − 1) sets the mark-up: the more elastic the demand, the smaller the mark-up.

L14 progress check: very elastic buyers and a strong network effect for sellers ⇒ low price or subsidy for buyers, higher price for sellers (answer B). Deriving the formula goes beyond the course; the intuition is enough for the exam.
If you ask “who pays on this platform?”, look for the side the other absolutely wants to find: it is often the one being subsidised.
Buyers have very elastic demand and strongly attract sellers. Which price structure?
Low price or subsidy for buyers, higher price for sellers
Both forces point the same way: high elasticity and a large benefit created for the other side.
High prices on both sides
That would drive away the elastic side and, with it, the value for sellers.
Equal prices on both sides
Nothing requires symmetry: each side has its own elasticity and its own effect on the other.
Concentration or coexistence: count the forces on each side

If everyone uses only one app and each new member attracts the other side, the market tips towards a single platform. But if people can keep several apps, if crowding slows the service or if network effects are weak, several platforms survive.

Lecture L14: towards concentration — positive between-group and within-group network effects, economies of scale, single-homing. Towards coexistence — multi-homing, congestion, weak network effects. On the platform, the owner is often “umpire and player”.
A network effect leads to monopoly only if users must choose: with multi-homing, the entrant does not have to win over the whole network.
The “umpire and player” sets the rules its competitors face: how information is displayed, higher fees for rivals.
L14 progress check: frequent congestion and negative within-group effects are what LEAST leads to concentration (answer C).
Faced with a digital market, tick both columns before concluding “winner takes all”.
Which LEAST leads to a market dominated by a single platform?
Frequent congestion and negative within-group effects
More users degrade the service: joining a competing platform becomes attractive.
Strong positive between-group network effects
They push towards concentration.
Single-homing by users
It pushes towards concentration: everyone must choose a single network.
High fixed costs and economies of scale
They favour the largest platform.
Four auctions: who pays what, in one round or several

In an auction room, the price rises until only one buyer is left. At the Dutch flower market, it falls until someone shouts “stop”. With a sealed envelope, you bid only once without seeing the others.

Lecture L14: dynamic and second price = English (ascending); dynamic and first price = Dutch (descending); static and second price = Vickrey; static and first price = first-price sealed bid. Private values (a non-resellable concert ticket) versus common value (drilling rights, risk of the winner’s curse).
English auction with reserve price r < v2 < v1: bidder 2 drops out at v2, bidder 1 wins and pays about v2, as in Vickrey.

In a first-price sealed-bid auction, bidder 1 maximises P(b1 > b2) × (v1 − b1): bidding more raises the chance of winning but cuts the gain, so they bid below their value and the object may go to the wrong buyer.
For the seller, more bidders and a good reserve price raise revenue. Google and Facebook use second-price variants for their ad slots.
First read two things in the question: does the winner pay their own bid or the second one? Are values private or common?
A descending auction where the first to accept pays the displayed price is:
A Dutch auction (dynamic, first price)
The price falls and the winner pays the price at which they stop it: their own “bid”.
An English auction
The English auction is ascending and the winner pays about the second value.
A Vickrey auction
Vickrey is static (sealed envelope) and second-price.
You value a ticket at €100 in a Vickrey auction (private values). Which bid?
Exactly €100
Your bid only decides whether you win; the payment is set by the second bid. Bidding your value is weakly dominant.
Slightly above €100 to be sure to win
You might pay between 100 and your bid, so more than your value.
About €80 to keep some surplus
The surplus comes from the second price; underbidding only makes you lose auctions you would have won profitably.

Teaching mini-exam built on E2020–E2025 and §14. The trade, tariff and auction numbers are documented/recalculated; the exchange of 3 drinks for 2 snacks is constructed. Based on lectures L13–L14; this answer is not official.
